title: The map: what ML really is

steps.sub: In a normal program, YOU write the rules. ML flips that: you show it examples, and it writes the rules itself. By the end you'll have a clean map — the three ways machines learn, and where each one lives in the real world.

steps.prompt: A normal program vs an ML model — what's the real difference?

options.t: ML runs faster than a normal program.
In a normal program YOU write the rules; an ML model learns the rules from data.
ML doesn't use code at all.

steps.why: That's the whole flip. To detect spam the old way, you'd hand-write rules ('if it says FREE MONEY…'). ML instead reads thousands of emails already labelled spam/not-spam and figures out the pattern itself. You bring examples; it writes the rules. Speed and code are beside the point.
hints: Who comes up with the rules — you, or the machine?
Think spam filter: do you list every spammy phrase, or show it examples and let it learn?

steps.prompt: Three ways a machine can learn.
steps.sub: Tap each card. These three cover almost everything in ML.

cards.b: Learn from labelled examples. Photos tagged 'cat'/'dog' → predict the label on a new photo. You give the answers.
No labels — find hidden structure on its own. e.g. group 10,000 customers into natural segments nobody defined.
Learn by reward. Try an action, get a score, do more of what scores well. How a game-playing or robot policy learns.

steps.prompt: Which kind of learning is each task?
steps.sub: Tap a task, then its bin.

items.t: Predict house price from past sales (each with its known price)
Group shoppers into segments nobody labelled in advance
Teach a drone to fly to a target — reward it for getting closer
Tell spam from not-spam, trained on emails already marked spam
Find natural clusters of songs with no genre tags

hints: Are the right answers (labels) given up front? → supervised.
No labels, just 'find the groups' → unsupervised. Learns from reward/score → RL.

steps.prompt: You have a million product photos with NO labels, and you want to discover natural groupings. Which approach?
steps.sub: Match the tool to the situation.
steps.why: No labels exist, and you're not rewarding actions — you just want hidden structure to surface. That's unsupervised (clustering). Supervised needs labels you don't have; RL needs a reward signal and actions, which there are none of here.
hints: Do you have any labels to learn from? Are there actions to reward?
No labels + no reward + 'find the groups' points at exactly one of the three.

steps.sub: Tap each, then check all at once.

statements.t: In supervised learning you must provide the correct answers (labels) to learn from.
statements.why: Yes — 'supervised' means a teacher's answers are present. Without labels it can't be supervised.

statements.t: Unsupervised learning needs a human to label every example first.
statements.why: The opposite — its whole point is working with UNlabelled data and finding structure itself.

statements.t: Reinforcement learning improves by trying actions and reacting to a reward signal.
statements.why: Right — try, get scored, lean toward what scores well. That's the RL loop.

statements.t: ChatGPT-style models are a totally separate fourth category, unrelated to these three.
statements.why: Not separate — they're built mostly on supervised learning (predict the next word) plus a dose of RL (from human feedback). They sit on this same map.

hints: Read each word literally: 'supervised' implies a supervisor's answers.
Which one learns from a reward instead of from given answers?

steps.prompt: Put a supervised project in order, from start to finish.
steps.sub: Tap the steps in the order they happen.
chips: Use it on brand-new data it never saw
Train: let the model learn the input→answer pattern
hints: You can't train before you have the labelled examples.
Gather data → train on it → then deploy on new, unseen data.

steps.prompt: Why this is the 'faculties of mind, made buildable'.
steps.sub: Tap each card — the bigger picture behind the map.

cards.b: Supervised learning = the mind's faculty of recognising — 'I've seen this kind of thing before, it's a cat.'
Unsupervised = seeing patterns and groupings nobody pointed out — the mind organising raw experience.
RL = the faculty of learning from results — touch the hot stove once, never again.

steps.prompt: Big-picture check: what's the one thing all three kinds of ML share?

options.t: They all improve from data/experience instead of from hand-written rules.

steps.why: That's the thread. Labels are only in supervised; games are only some RL. But all three share the core flip from lesson one — they get better from data or experience rather than from rules a human typed out by hand.
hints: Two of these are true for only ONE of the three kinds.
Go back to the very first idea: where do the rules come from?

steps.sub: Not graded. Naming a real example from your world makes the rest of this course click.

fields.label: What do you work on or study most?
fields.ph: e.g. run a Shopify store / CS student / marketing

fields.label: Name one thing in YOUR world ML could learn — and guess which of the three it'd be:
fields.ph: e.g. predict which customers will churn — supervised

steps.prompt: Lock it in: tap EVERY true statement about ML.
steps.sub: Some are tempting but wrong. Pick only the true ones.
chips: The model learns rules from data
RL learns from a reward signal
ML is just a faster normal program with the same hand-written rules
steps.why: True: it learns rules from data, supervised uses labels, RL learns from reward. False: unsupervised needs NO labels, and ML is fundamentally different from a normal program — the machine writes the rules, you don't.
hints: Two of these contradict things you just sorted.
Recall: who writes the rules, and which kind of learning has no labels?
